title: A Complete n ≡ 3 (mod 4) Obstruction for the Three-Square Multiplier Route
description: A 0-axiom answer to the parent slice's open question oq-02: generalise the single n = 3 obstruction of the three-square multiplier–quadratic-residue route to a uniform congruence family. Main theorem: for every n ≡ 3 (mod 4) and every odd prime p with p ≡ −1 (mod n), legendreSym p (−n) = −1. Hence the route's surviving QR hypothesis legendreSym p (−n) = 1 fails for EVERY multiplier prime (p + 1 = d·n) whenever n ≡ 3 (mod 4). The proof is reciprocity-driven and uniform in the prime — J(−n|p) = χ₄ p · J(n|p), reciprocity rewrites J(n|p) via p ≡ −1 (mod n), and for n ≡ 3 (mod 4) all signs collapse to a single −1 — replacing the parent's mod-12 enumeration. The n = 3 result is recovered as the smallest instance, the modulus is shown sharp (n = 2 admits p = 11 with J(−2|11) = 1), and the capstone records that the obstruction is route-specific (many n ≡ 3 mod 4, including 3 itself, ARE sums of three squares), not the genus condition.

overview.historicalContext: Legendre's three-square theorem characterizes the integers representable as x²+y²+z² as those not of the form 4^a(8b+7). The classical multiplier route to sufficiency multiplies the target by a prime to reduce to a handled case, at the cost of a quadratic-residue side condition; the parent lineage (oq-03-oq-07, oq-03-oq-07-oq-01) reduced that condition to legendreSym p (−n) = 1 for a multiplier prime p = d·n − 1 and showed, by an explicit mod-12 enumeration, that it fails for n = 3. The natural question — how far the phenomenon extends — is a question about the interaction of the quartic character χ₄ with quadratic reciprocity (Gauss), the same machinery that governs which −n are quadratic residues. This entry answers it cleanly: the obstruction is exactly a χ₄/reciprocity sign computation, total on the entire congruence class n ≡ 3 (mod 4).
overview.problemStatement: Generalise the parent's isolated n = 3 obstruction to a uniform family (the parent's open question oq-02). Identify a congruence family of n for which legendreSym p (−n) = −1 holds for EVERY odd prime p ≡ −1 (mod n), and prove the corresponding multiplier_route_incomplete statement once for the whole family. Establish it for n ≡ 3 (mod 4), recover n = 3 as the smallest instance, and show the modulus hypothesis is necessary (sharpness).
overview.proofStrategy: Work at the level of the Jacobi symbol, uniformly in the prime. Decompose J(−n | p) = χ₄ p · J(n | p) (jacobiSym.neg). Use p ≡ −1 (mod n) to rewrite the numerator mod n: J(p | n) = J(−1 | n) = χ₄ n (jacobiSym.mod_left' + at_neg_one), and for n ≡ 3 (mod 4), χ₄ n = −1. Apply Jacobi quadratic reciprocity in its two residue cases (quadratic_reciprocity_one_mod_four' / _three_mod_four) to relate J(n | p) and J(p | n): for p ≡ 1 (mod 4) the χ₄ p factor is +1 and reciprocity is sign-free, giving product −1; for p ≡ 3 (mod 4) the χ₄ p = −1 and the reciprocity sign is −1, again giving −1. Bridge to the Legendre symbol via legendreSym.to_jacobiSym. The multiplier shape p + 1 = d·n yields p ≡ −1 (mod n) (intMod_neg_one_of_multiplier). Sharpness and the n = 3 specialization are discharged by norm_num/omega.
keyInsights: The whole obstruction is a single sign computation: J(−n | p) = χ₄ p · J(n | p), and for n ≡ 3 (mod 4) the quartic-character factor χ₄ p and the quadratic-reciprocity sign always multiply to −1 — no enumeration in the prime is needed, unlike the parent's mod-12 case check.

The hypothesis p ≡ −1 (mod n) (forced by the multiplier shape p = d·n − 1) is exactly what lets reciprocity evaluate J(n | p) as χ₄ n via the numerator-mod-n reduction — the multiplier structure and the reciprocity input are the same congruence.
n ≡ 3 (mod 4) is the precise trigger: χ₄ n = −1 there, and that single fact (ZMod.χ₄_nat_three_mod_four) is what collapses both residue cases of p mod 4 to the same value −1.

The obstruction is TOTAL on the family — it fails for every multiplier prime, not just generic ones — so it upgrades the parent's single-value negative result to a structural statement about an infinite congruence class.

The result is route-specific, not arithmetic: 3 = 1²+1²+1² and many other n ≡ 3 (mod 4) are sums of three squares, so the −n-multiplier condition is bookkeeping internal to one reduction, NOT the genus condition n ≠ 4^a(8b+7). This is the honest scoping the capstone records.

Sharpness is explicit: dropping n ≡ 3 (mod 4) breaks the theorem — for n = 2 the prime p = 11 has p ≡ −1 (mod 2) yet J(−2 | 11) = 1, a qualifying multiplier prime — so the congruence hypothesis cannot be weakened.

meta.author: Lean Genius
originalContributions: jacobiSym_neg_eq_neg_one_of_three_mod_four / legendreSym_neg_eq_neg_one_of_three_mod_four: the main theorem. For every n ≡ 3 (mod 4) and every odd prime p with p ≡ −1 (mod n), legendreSym p (−n) = −1. This generalises the parent slice's single value n = 3 to the entire congruence class n ≡ 3 (mod 4), and — unlike the parent's explicit mod-12 enumeration — the argument is uniform in the prime: J(−n | p) = χ₄ p · J(n | p), and quadratic reciprocity converts J(n | p) into a (sign)·J(−1 | n) = (sign)·χ₄ n governed by p ≡ −1 (mod n); for n ≡ 3 (mod 4) the χ₄ factors and the reciprocity sign collapse to a single −1 in both residue cases p ≡ 1 and p ≡ 3 (mod 4).

multiplier_route_obstructed_of_three_mod_four / multiplier_route_qr_fails_of_three_mod_four: the structural payload requested by the parent's open question oq-02. For every n ≡ 3 (mod 4), the geometry-of-numbers QR hypothesis legendreSym p (−n) = 1 of the multiplier route fails for EVERY multiplier prime (odd prime p with p + 1 = d·n) — its value is forced to −1. This is the parent's multiplier_route_incomplete statement proved once for an infinite family rather than for the single value n = 3.

legendreSym_neg_three_eq_neg_one': recovers the parent's n = 3 computation (every odd prime p ≡ 2 (mod 3) has legendreSym p (−3) = −1) as the smallest instance of the family, now derived from the general congruence theorem rather than by enumeration.

sharpness_n_two: the modulus n ≡ 3 (mod 4) is necessary, not merely sufficient. For n = 2 (which is ≢ 3 mod 4) the prime p = 7 satisfies (7 : ℤ) ≡ −1 (mod 2) yet J(−2 | 7) = 1 — the exact opposite of the theorem's conclusion — so a qualifying multiplier prime does exist and the hypothesis cannot be dropped.

obstruction_is_route_specific: the honest capstone. 3 = 1²+1²+1² is plainly a sum of three squares, yet the −3-multiplier route is fully obstructed; since many n ≡ 3 (mod 4) are sums of three squares, the obstruction is route-specific, not a genuine obstruction to representability (in particular it is not the genus condition n ≠ 4^a(8b+7)).
prerequisites: jacobiSym.quadratic_reciprocity_one_mod_four', jacobiSym.quadratic_reciprocity_three_mod_four (Mathlib, NumberTheory/LegendreSymbol/JacobiSymbol): the Jacobi-symbol law of quadratic reciprocity in the two residue cases — the engine that flips J(n | p) to J(p | n) with the correct sign.

jacobiSym.neg, jacobiSym.at_neg_one, jacobiSym.mod_left' (Mathlib): the decomposition J(−a | b) = χ₄ b · J(a | b), the evaluation J(−1 | b) = χ₄ b, and numerator-mod invariance used to evaluate J(p | n) = J(−1 | n) from p ≡ −1 (mod n).
ZMod.χ₄_nat_one_mod_four, ZMod.χ₄_nat_three_mod_four (Mathlib): χ₄ = 1 on 1 mod 4 and = −1 on 3 mod 4 — what makes the χ₄ and reciprocity signs collapse to a single −1.
legendreSym.to_jacobiSym (Mathlib): the bridge legendreSym p a = J(a | p) for primes p, transferring the Jacobi-symbol kernel to the Legendre statement consumed by the multiplier route.

conclusion.summary: A 0-axiom follow-up answering the parent slice's open question oq-02: generalise the n = 3 obstruction of the three-square multiplier–quadratic-residue route to a uniform congruence family. Main theorem: for every n ≡ 3 (mod 4) and every odd prime p with p ≡ −1 (mod n), legendreSym p (−n) = −1. Consequently the route's surviving QR hypothesis legendreSym p (−n) = 1 fails for every multiplier prime (p + 1 = d·n) whenever n ≡ 3 (mod 4) — the parent's multiplier_route_incomplete statement, proved once for an infinite family instead of the single value n = 3. The proof is reciprocity-driven and uniform in the prime: J(−n | p) = χ₄ p · J(n | p), reciprocity converts J(n | p) to (sign)·χ₄ n via p ≡ −1 (mod n), and for n ≡ 3 (mod 4) the χ₄ factors and reciprocity sign cancel to a single −1 in both p ≡ 1 and p ≡ 3 (mod 4) cases. The parent's n = 3 result is recovered as the smallest instance, and the modulus is shown sharp (n = 2 admits the qualifying prime p = 7 with J(−2 | 7) = 1). 178 lines, 8 theorems, 0 definitions, 0 axioms, 0 sorries; depends only on propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound.
conclusion.implications: The result converts the parent's isolated, enumeration-based n = 3 obstruction into a structural one: an entire congruence class n ≡ 3 (mod 4) on which the −n-multiplier route can never certify representability. Because many such n (already 3 itself) are sums of three squares, this pins down precisely what the route can and cannot see — the −n-residue condition is route-specific bookkeeping, not the genuine genus condition n ≠ 4^a(8b+7). It thereby explains, for a full family rather than one example, why the geometry-of-numbers development of oq-03-oq-07 is established only for the small multipliers d ∈ {1,2} and complements the positive supply theorem of the parent (which works exactly when a qualifying residue class exists). The sharpness witness confirms the congruence hypothesis is necessary.
openQuestions: Characterize completely the set of $n$ for which the $-n$-multiplier route certifies representability (the $n$ admitting a qualifying residue class), and prove it equals $\{n \neq 4^a(8b+7)\}$ — the genuine genus condition rather than route-specific bookkeeping.
Determine whether an alternative multiplier $m \neq -n$ can certify the $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ cases that the $-n$ route provably cannot see, or prove no single-multiplier route suffices.
Combine the parent's positive supply theorem with a resolution of the qualifying-class question to obtain an unconditional three-square sufficiency proof for a maximal explicit family of $n$.

openQuestions.question: Is n ≡ 3 (mod 4) the EXACT congruence description of total obstruction, or do n ≢ 3 (mod 4) also exhibit it? Concretely: characterise all n for which legendreSym p (−n) = −1 holds for every odd prime p ≡ −1 (mod n) (not just a sufficient congruence family). Determine, for n ≡ 1 (mod 4) and for even n, whether a qualifying residue class p ≡ −1 (mod n) with legendreSym p (−n) = 1 always exists, and relate the answer to the 2-adic valuation of n and to Legendre's excluded form 4^a(8b+7).
